title: 3 days Upper 2 days Lower program review (for an advanced calisthenics guy part. 2)
summary: NH finishes reviewing Lawrence's 3-upper/2-lower program for an advanced calisthenics athlete chasing a golden-era physique. He wants lower reps on weighted pull-ups and dips, fewer redundant presses, more hip hinging and a dedicated deadlift, weighted rather than technical calisthenics, and real progression on arms, traps and legs.
claims: Spread rest days through the week (e.g. 2 on, 1 off, 3 on) rather than five days in a row then two off; you don't need two full days to recover
On three days a week, alternate training and rest days for full recovery and to raise frequency, volume and intensity
If you only rest once a week, place it after the heavy lower-body days at the end of the week
A rest day isn't a couch day: do mobility, cardio, swimming or neglected parts like calves, neck and forearms
For an advanced calisthenics athlete, weighted pull-ups for 10-15 reps are too light; use 3 sets of 3-5, 4-6 or 6-10 to force adaptation
Weighted pull-ups and dips are strength movements and should be trained with higher intensity and lower volume
Weighted pull-ups and dips barely tax the cardiovascular system, so you can superset them with light work like calves, neck, forearms or shoulders
Do chest-supported rows on an incline bench: a flat bench limits the lat stretch and the incline arm angle hits the upper back differently
Chest-supported dumbbell rows are much harder than normal rows because you can't use your legs; if you max out the dumbbells, add fat grips
Don't put heavy dips and heavy barbell bench in the same session; both are very demanding on the shoulders
If dumbbells are too light, use flies or slow negatives to make pressing harder
Three press movements in one workout is redundant; pick one or two and progress on them
One-arm lateral raises leaning away from a pole are the best version because they remove the traps and focus on side and rear delts
Arms need progression, intensity and volume like any other muscle; pump work alone won't grow them
Superset a heavy biceps or long-head triceps movement with weighted pull-ups or rows to save time
Sissy squats are hard on the knees because of exaggerated knee flexion; anything that can grow a muscle can damage the structure around it
Use 10-15 reps on risky movements so you can sense the rep that would injure you; with 3-5 it's harder to see coming
Load hyperextensions and progress them for 8-12 reps; bodyweight versions eventually stop stimulating the lower back and glutes
Hip hinges should be included whenever you can tolerate them; they also give free upper-back hypertrophy
Prefer a hip hinge over leg curls: leg curls only grow the hamstrings, hinges give much more hypertrophy
If you test a deadlift max, you need a day dedicated to deadlifting, e.g. open the second lower day with it
Compound lower-body movements are the best way to grow legs; legs grow as long as you find a way to train them without injury
Bodyweight calisthenics cost so little recovery that they can be spread through other days instead of taking a full day
End sessions with easy giant sets for pump and work capacity, but this isn't your main means of progression
An athlete who has mastered calisthenics should weight those movements rather than repeat them at unchallenging reps
Calisthenics athletes look like calisthenics athletes, not bodybuilders; you need upper-back thickness from heavy pulls, shrugs and rows, plus legs, calves and arms
